questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'final cheat sheet' at the end of a lesson like this?
options: To condense every important formula and rule from the lesson into one compact, easily-reviewable reference
To introduce brand-new material
To replace the need for practice sets
To only summarize the first two parts of the lesson
questions.rationale: A final cheat sheet condenses all the important formulas and rules covered throughout the lesson into one compact, quickly-reviewable reference.

questions.question: Why does the lesson include separate 'Practice Set — Basic, Intermediate, Advanced' tiers?
options: To make the lesson longer without added value
Because basic and advanced problems use entirely different formulas
To let learners build up their skill progressively, rather than jumping straight to the hardest problems
Tiered practice sets serve no pedagogical purpose
questions.rationale: Tiered practice sets let learners build skill progressively, reinforcing fundamentals before tackling the most difficult, composite-figure-heavy problems.

questions.question: What is the value of including 'Answers' sections directly after each practice set?
options: It removes the need to actually attempt the problems
It lets learners immediately check their work and catch mistakes while the problem is still fresh in mind
It has no real pedagogical value
It only benefits advanced learners
questions.rationale: Immediate answer-checking lets learners catch and understand mistakes while the problem and their reasoning are still fresh, reinforcing the correct method faster.

questions.question: What might an 'Important Exam Warning' in this lesson likely caution against?
options: Using formulas at all
Using coordinate models
Practicing with basic problems first
Relying on a single memorized formula without checking whether the specific figure actually matches the formula's assumptions
questions.rationale: Consistent with the lesson's recurring theme, such a warning would caution against blindly applying a memorized formula to a figure that doesn't actually match its assumptions.

questions.question: What is meant by the lesson's 'Deep Concept' section, based on the lesson's overall theme?
options: That reliable figure counting comes from systematic, verifiable methods rather than visual intuition or memorized shortcuts alone
That figure counting cannot be taught systematically
That only formulas matter, not understanding
That every figure-counting problem is unsolvable without a computer
questions.rationale: The lesson's consistent theme throughout is that systematic, verifiable methods — not visual intuition or blind memorization — are what make figure counting reliable.

questions.question: Why are 'quick reference values' (like squares in a 3x3 or 4x4 grid) useful to have memorized separately from the formulas themselves?
options: They are not actually useful to know separately
They replace the need to understand any formula
They let you instantly verify common cases without recalculating the formula every time
They only apply to rectangles, not squares
questions.rationale: Having common values memorized provides an instant way to verify a calculation against a known case, without needing to recompute the formula from scratch every time.

questions.question: What is the benefit of tiered practice sets (basic to advanced) paired with answers, as a study method?
options: It has no measurable benefit
It reinforces correct technique at each difficulty level before compounding that technique in harder, more complex figures
It only benefits students who skip the basic tier
It replaces the need for the earlier formula sections entirely
questions.rationale: Progressing through tiers with immediate answer-checking reinforces correct technique at each level before applying that same technique to increasingly complex figures.

questions.question: Why might a 'deep concept' section be placed near the very end of a long lesson rather than at the beginning?
options: Its placement is arbitrary and has no reasoning behind it
Because deep concepts are always the easiest material
Because it introduces material unrelated to the rest of the lesson
Because it's meant to consolidate understanding after all the individual techniques and formulas have already been introduced and practiced
questions.rationale: Placing conceptual consolidation near the end lets it draw on and unify everything already introduced and practiced, rather than being presented before the learner has the necessary context.

questions.question: What general principle underlies most of the 'quick reference values' given throughout this lesson?
options: That every figure requires a unique, unrelated formula
That regular, well-structured figures (like grids) follow predictable formulas that can be verified and reused
That reference values are only useful for triangles
That formulas cannot be verified against specific cases
questions.rationale: The quick reference values reflect the broader principle that regular, well-structured figures follow predictable formulas — these values are just specific, verifiable instances of those general formulas.

questions.question: Why is it useful to memorize a few key reference values (like 14 squares in a 3x3 grid) even if you also know the general formula?
options: It isn't useful, the formula alone is always sufficient
It provides a fast sanity check against which to verify a longer calculation during time-pressured exam conditions
It replaces the need to ever use the formula again
It only matters for figures larger than 4x4
questions.rationale: A memorized reference value provides an instant sanity check against a freshly-calculated result, which is especially valuable under exam time pressure.
